questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{FG}$ traversed from the point $F(1,0)$ to the point $G(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}x\,dx-xy\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=i$ and $b=2\,i+3\,j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =i+t(2\,i+3\,j-i) \\  & =i+t(i+3\,j) \\  & =(1+t)\,i+3t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=1+t$ and $y(t)=3t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+3\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx-xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(1+t)\cdot 1-(1+t)\cdot 3t\cdot 3\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}1-8t-9{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={[t-4{t}^{2}-3{t}^{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[1-4(1)^{2}-3(1)^{3}]-[0] \\  & =-6\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overset{―}{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(1,1),$ then ${\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y\,dx-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $a=0\,i+0\,j$ and $b=i+j.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =0\,i+0\,j+t(i+j-(0\,i+0\,j)) \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0\le t\le 1.$ Thus, we have that $x(t)=t$ and $y(t)=t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y\,dx-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t\cdot 1-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t-\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t\,dt \\  & ={[-\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi t}{\pi }-\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi t}{\pi }]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =-\frac{1}{\pi }[\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi )-\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)] \\  & =-\frac{1}{\pi }[-1+0-1-0] \\  & =\frac{2}{\pi }\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: If the path $C$ is a part of the graph $y={x}^{2}-1$ traversed from the point $P(1,0)$ to point $Q(2,3),$ then ${\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy=$
questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}-1.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+({t}^{2}-1)\,j,\,t\in [1,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{y}^{2}\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}({y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{({t}^{2}-1)}^{2}\cdot 1+t\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}-2{t}^{2}+1+2{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{2}{t}^{4}+1\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{5}}{5}+t]}_{1}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{5}}{5}+2]-[\frac{{1}^{5}}{5}+1] \\  & =\frac{32}{5}+2-\frac{1}{5}-1 \\  & =\frac{36}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y={x}^{2}.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,2]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}x\,dx+y\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+y\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t\cdot 1+{t}^{2}\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}t+2{t}^{3}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =[\frac{{2}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{2}^{4}}{2}]-[0] \\  & =2+8 \\  & =10\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=2$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(\sqrt{2},0)$ to the point $B(0,\sqrt{2}).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the parametrization of the curve $C.$ Since it's a circle if radius $\sqrt{2}$ centered at the origin, the curve $C$ can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, along the curve we have that $x(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,i+\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx-x\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}-x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-\sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot \sqrt{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}(-2{sin}^{2}⁡t-2{cos}^{2}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & =-2{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\text{d}t \\  & =-2t{|}_{0}^{\pi /2} \\  & =-2[\frac{\pi }{2}-0] \\  & =-\pi \end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Evaluate ${\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy,$ where $C$ is part of the circle ${x}^{2}+{y}^{2}=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $A(-2,0)$ to the point $B(0,-2).$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we need to find the parametrization of the curve $C.$ Since it's a circle if radius $2$ centered at the origin, the curve $C$ can be parametrized as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,j,\,t\in [\pi ,\frac{3\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, along the curve we have that $x(t)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t$ and $y(t)=2\operatorname{sin}⁡t.$ 

The derivative of $r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡(t)\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡(t)\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}y\,dx+x\,dy & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(y\,\frac{dx}{\text{d}t}+x\,\frac{dy}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\cdot (-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}(-4{sin}^{2}⁡t+4{cos}^{2}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}({cos}^{2}⁡t-{sin}^{2}⁡t)\text{d}t \\  & =4{\int }_{\pi }^{3\pi /2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2t)\,\text{d}t \\  & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡2t{|}_{\pi }^{3\pi /2} \\  & =2[\operatorname{sin}⁡(3\pi )-\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\pi )] \\  & =2(0-0) \\  & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Over Segments
canonical_examples.problem:
If the path $C$ is the line segment $\overline{AB}$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(1, 1),$ calculate the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int\limits_C x^2y\,\mathrm{d}x + xy\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
The position vectors of the endpoints of our line segment are $\mathbf{a} = 0\,\mathbf{i} + 0\,\mathbf{j}$ and $\mathbf{b} = 1\,\mathbf{i} + 1\,\mathbf{j}.$ So, the parametrization of the line segment is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =a+t\,(b-a) \\  & =t\,i+t\,j,\end{aligned}
$$

where $0 \le t \le 1.$ So, we have that $x(t) = t$ and $y(t) = t$ along the segment.

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}{x}^{2}y\,dx+xy\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({x}^{2}y\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+xy\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{2}\cdot t\cdot 1+t\cdot t\cdot 1\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{t}^{3}+{t}^{2}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{4}}{4}+\frac{{t}^{3}}{3}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}+\frac{1}{3} \\  & =\frac{7}{12}\end{aligned}
$$

Example: 
                    Evaluating Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Cartesian Curves
canonical_examples.problem:
If the path $C$ is a part of the parabola $y=x^2$ traversed from the point $A(0,0)$ to the point $B(1,1),$ evaluate the line integral 

$$
\displaystyle \int\limits_C (x+y)\,\mathrm{d}x + (x-y)\,\mathrm{d}y.
$$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Notice that our curve is given by the explicit Cartesian equation $y = x^2.$ As a result, we obtain the following parametrization of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t)=x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=t\,i+{t}^{2}\,j,\,t\in [0,1]\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$ is given by

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j=i+2t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now evaluate the line integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(x+y)\,dx+(x-y)\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}((x+y)\,\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+(x-y)\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(t+{t}^{2})\cdot 1+(t-{t}^{2})\cdot 2t\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}t+3{t}^{2}-2{t}^{3}\,dt \\  & ={[\frac{{t}^{2}}{2}+{t}^{3}-\frac{{t}^{4}}{2}]}_{0}^{1} \\  & =[\frac{1}{2}+1-\frac{1}{2}]-[0] \\  & =1\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.name:
Example: 
                    Computing Line Integrals With Respect to X and Y Along Circles and Ellipses
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/multivariable/14119190/assets/7a6e67435aab40d5bf3630c66f79241008357e1549b1c77b4c0bdfea2b453883.png)

Evaluate $\displaystyle \int\limits_C \dfrac{y\,\mathrm{d}x - x\,\mathrm{d}y}{x^2+y^2},$ where $C$ is a part of the circle $x^2+y^2=4$ traversed in the counterclockwise direction from the point $(2,0)$ to the point $\left(0,2\right).$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
First, notice that a parametrization for the given path is

$$
\begin{aligned}r(t) & =x(t)\,i+y(t)\,j=2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,j,\,t\in [0,\frac{\pi }{2}].\end{aligned}
$$

The derivative of $\mathbf r(t)$  is

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & ={x}^{′}(t)\,i+{y}^{′}(t)\,j=-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+2\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can calculate the line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\frac{y\,dx-x\,dy}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}} & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{y\cdot {x}^{′}-x\cdot {y}^{′}}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)-(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)}{(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}+(2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}},dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{-4{sin}^{2}⁡t-4{cos}^{2}⁡t}{4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,dt \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\frac{-4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)}{4({cos}^{2}⁡t+{sin}^{2}⁡t)}\,dt \\  & =-{\int }_{0}^{\pi /2}\,dt \\  & =-\frac{\pi }{2}\end{aligned}
$$

tutorials.name: Introduction
tutorials.problem:
Let $f(x,y)$ be a function of two variables and $C$ be a path in the $xy$-plane. Recall that the line integral

$$
\int\limits_C f(x,y) \, \textrm dx +  f(x,y)\,\textrm d y
$$

can be evaluated by parameterizing $C$ using the parameter $t\in [a,b]$ and then applying a change of variables, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}x+f(x,y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{a}^{b}f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t+f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{a}^{b}(f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}+f(x,y)\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})\,\text{d}t\end{aligned}
$$

The hardest part is often finding a suitable parameterization for curve $C.$ We'll discuss a number of different cases in this lesson.
